A planetary transit occurs when a planet passes
between Earth and the Sun. For a study, student groups
in 6 locations worldwide observed the times at which
Venus moved into specific reference positions during its
June 2004 transit. Figure 1 shows 4 reference positions
(first, second, third, and fourth contacts) along the transit
At each viewing location, the transit was
observed using telescopes with solar filters, which only
allow the transmission of light with a wavelength of
656 nanometers (nm). Students at each location used a
clock calibrated to Coordinated Universal Time (referred
to as UTC), the time at Earth’s 0° longitude, to record the
time at which Venus was observed in the second and third
contact positions. The ability to view the full transit
required that the Sun be above the horizon during the
entire transit and that the local weather not interfere with a
clear view of the Sun. Table 1 shows the UTC times
(hr:min:s) that the second and third contact positions were
observed by groups at each location.
